hero.filename: Japanese Occupation Photo of West Coast Sumatra.jpg
hero.caption:
In the front row, in the centre was the very famous General, the Ruler of the Southern Region, Field Marshall Hisaichi Terauchi who was based in Singapore. To Terauchi's right was General Tanabe, Commander of the 25th Division based in Bukittinggi. To Terauchi's left is none other than Governor Yano.

Original caption: Japanese Staff Officers for the Southern Areas: front from left to right, Nishiooeda, General Tanabe (Head of the 25th Army), General Terauchi, Yano (a civilian officer, the shu—chokan of West Sumatra) .

images.caption: Letter from Taisei-Yokusankai, inviting Madjid to come from Kofu to Tokyo, dated May 4, 1945, for a meeting on May 8. Madjid was living in Kofu under house arrest barred from exiting the city. It was not until 1945 until he was called by the Taisei-Yokusankai in a correspondance set at 8 May 1945. The purpose was for Madjid to lead a "Interim Indonesian Government" once Japan agrees to follow through the Koiso Promise. Madjid refused.

images.filename: Group picture of the Kutacane Political Prisoners, 1942.jpg
images.caption:
At the height of the Pacific War, the people of West Sumatra tried to demonstrate so that the Dutch turned over authority to the people instead of to the Japanese. The leaders of the movement Such as Chatib Sulaiman (sitting second front row from right) was arrested and held at Kuta Cane (Aceh). 
Standing at the back were former KNIL soldiers who were guarding them.

Standing at the back were former KNIL soldiers who were guarding them.

images.caption: Japanese soldiers still seen wandering and occupying the City of Bukittinggi after the Proclamation of Indonesia’s Independence and the Surrender of Japan. During so the British Indian 26th infantry have yet to reach Bukittinggi. According to a newsletter from 13 February 1946, many of the Japanese inland still occupies the Sumatran inland regions (highlands) and are still armed. Some on the coast collaborated with the allies in peacekeeping.

images.filename: Yano Kenzo posing with Traditional dressed Minangkabau women.jpg
images.caption: Yano Kenzo and a Japanese officer posing with traditionally dressed Minangkabau women. Yano Kenzo was not a Soldier, instead, he donned this soldier's outfit and samurai sword for the professional mandatory Photo-op. He was curious and fascinated with the Minangkabau tradition. Especially the unique Matrilineal tradition of the Minangkabau. According to his book, he disliked wearing the outfit.
images.alt: Yano Kenzo and a Japanese officer posing with traditionally dressed Minangkabau women.
